To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) early experience with pain is associated with altered pain responsiveness; (2) the nature of this altered responsiveness varies with the infant’s developmental state and cumulative pain history; (3) the altered pain responsiveness is not a permanent change in pain threshold, but rather a temporary change in pain reactivity; and (4) analgesic agents administered during the painful procedure reduce pain and its long-term effects.

(1) early experiences of noxious procedures are associated with changes in pain behaviors in infancy, and (2) analgesic agents administered during the early experience of noxious stimuli reduce the magnitude of long term changes in pain behavior.

(a) early pain experiences are associated with long-term changes in infant pain responses, (b) the direction of the long-term changes in the pain response depends, in large part, on the neonatal developmental stage, the type and duration of the pain stimulus, and the cumulative pain experience of the infant, and (c) the long-term effects of early pain experiences are reduced by the administration of local anesthetics and opioids.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term effects of early pain experience on subsequent pain responses.
the effects of pain on the developing nervous system.
the effects of early pain experience in newborn infants on pain responses later in life.

neonatal pain experiences can alter subsequent pain responses in infants and children.

the long-term effects of pain are dependent on many factors including: the type, duration, and frequency of the noxious stimuli, the infant’s developmental state and the infant’s prior experience with pain.

the effects of early pain experience on later pain response are complex and depend on the type of noxious stimulus (e.g., surgical vs procedural), the developmental stage of the individual, and his/her cumulative pain experience.

the effects of early painful experience are complex and depend on the type, frequency, and timing of the pain experience, the age of the infant at the time of pain exposure, and the type of analgesic agent used.
the experience of early pain can have long-lasting effects on the infant’s pain response.
early painful experiences in the perinateral period have a significant impact on subsequent pain responses.

pain is a significant stressor for neonates and infants, and that pain experiences in infancy may have long-term consequences.
pain is an experience that has the capacity to change how the nervous system responds to pain.
the pain experienced in infancy is a significant predictor of pain responses later in life.
